nameStory: This tiny sea slug gets its 'glassy-bubble' name from its translucent, bubble-like shell that you can see right through, like a miniature glass ornament. The 'solitary' part refers to how these little creatures are usually found alone rather than in groups, quietly going about their business on the seafloor.
description: The Solitary Glassy-bubble is a tiny sea slug with a delicate, see-through shell that looks like a small glass bead. This marine mollusk typically measures only about 3-5 millimeters long—smaller than your pinky nail. Unlike the colorful sea slugs you might picture, this one keeps things simple with its clear, bubble-shaped shell and pale body. It's actually a type of bubble snail that spends its life crawling along sandy and muddy ocean bottoms.

idTips.label: Transparent shell
idTips.description: The shell is completely see-through like glass, allowing you to see the animal's body parts inside—hold it up to light and it practically glows

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Extremely small at 3-5mm long, about the size of a small seed or grain of rice—easy to overlook among beach debris

idTips.label: Bubble shape
idTips.description: Shell is rounded and inflated like a tiny balloon, smooth to the touch with no ridges or bumps

idTips.label: Pale body
idTips.description: The soft body visible through the shell appears whitish or cream-colored, sometimes with faint dark spots

idTips.label: Found alone
idTips.description: Unlike many sea creatures, you'll typically find just one at a time rather than clusters or groups

habitat: Look for Solitary Glassy-bubbles in shallow coastal waters along New England's sandy and muddy bottoms, especially in protected bays and quiet inlets. They prefer areas where fine sediments accumulate, often near eelgrass beds or in shallow tide pools where they can burrow and feed. You're most likely to spot their tiny shells washed up on beaches after storms, particularly on Cape Cod and the islands.

seasonality.spring: Active season begins as waters warm, though they're difficult to spot due to their tiny size. Best chance is finding fresh shells on beaches after spring storms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most active in shallow waters. Look for them in tide pools during low tides, or check beach wrack lines for their delicate shells.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Autumn storms may wash shells ashore more frequently.
seasonality.winter: Much less active in cold water, retreating to deeper areas. Finding shells becomes more rare, though possible after major winter storms.

funFact: Despite having a shell, the Solitary Glassy-bubble can actually swim by flapping wing-like extensions of its foot—imagine a tiny underwater butterfly made of jelly propelling itself through the water column!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other tiny bubble shells or even small pieces of sea glass on the beach. The key difference is that this shell has a definite spiral structure when viewed closely, unlike smooth sea glass, and it's much more fragile—real sea glass won't crush between your fingers like these delicate shells will.
contextualKnowledge: **Note: Information about this rare species is limited, and some details should be verified with local marine biology resources.** These creatures belong to a group called bubble snails, which despite their name, are actually sea slugs that retained their shells through evolution.
compareHints: Since this is the only Haminella species in New England waters, compare it to other bubble snails in the family. Unlike the more common bubble shells you might find, Solitary Glassy-bubbles are much smaller and more perfectly transparent. Other bubble snails in the area tend to be larger, less transparent, or have more obvious shell patterns and colors.
